title: New (Final) Rules in Mental Health Parity: I
subtitle: Join Dr. Owen Muir as he evaluates the rule making adventures of the Federal Government.
text:
Oh my gosh. I am so excited. This is the first part of my series on the new final rules related to mental health parity. A while back, in the good ‘ole days of 2023, the Department of Labor and HHS issued a proposed rule related to mental health parity. I don’t want to brag, but I wrote four classic hip-hop-themed articles advocating soliciting open comments:

Shaggy: “It Wasn’t Me”

TLC: “No Scrubs”

Destiny: “Say My Name”

Macklemore + Ryan Lewis: “Thrift Shop”

And one non-hip-hop themed article, including the math I hoped DOL would advocate using:

Mental Health Parity Enforcement Made Simple

Suffice it to say: I was hoping the final rule drop would be hot.

This will be a thrilling breakdown of the updates to important federal rules. I’ll try to keep you awake—I promise.

Subscribe now

The Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act proposed that health plans have equivalent coverage standards for mental health and substance use (MH/SUD) care compared to medical/surgical care. However, the definitions of terms like “should,” “have,” “equivalent,” “coverage,” “standards,” “mental health and substance use,” “care,” and “medical/surgical” were all left inexactly defined, so there has been no meaningful enforcement. According to the final rule, the far too wordy purpose of the law is:

to ensure that participants and beneficiaries in a group health plan or in group health insurance coverage offered by a health insurance issuer that offers mental health or substance use disorder benefits are not subject to greater restrictions when seeking those benefits than when seeking medical/surgical benefits under the terms of the plan or coverage

That’s a mouthful! I might have said, “to ensure mental health coverage is not worse than other coverage.” This is why I don’t have a cushy government job, clearly.

The Department of Labor is attempting, along with HHS and other agencies, to change that by tightening standards. It’s a 536-page document. I’m doing my best to understand key points and communicate them to you, starting with:

What Counts as a Mental Health/Substance Use Disorder?

• If it is in ICD (the International Classification of Disease System, currently used in the US as ICD-10) or DSM (the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual). In that case, it’s included — including dementia and autism.

As noted in a footnote:

As discussed later in this preamble, the Departments stated in the proposed rules and reiterate in these final rules that ASD is a mental health condition for purposes of MHPAEA. (footnote 50, p. 21)

This is a huge deal, financially, because, according to UC Davis:

Their forecasts for ASD-related medical, nonmedical and productivity losses are $268 billion for 2015 and $461 billion for 2025. The researchers noted that these estimates are conservative and, if ASD prevalence continues to increase as it has in recent years, the costs could reach $1 trillion by 2025.

Further, once the DSM or ICD is updated, whichever is more recent, and a “new” mental health diagnosis exists, that becomes part of what needs to be covered within 60 days of its publication in the federal register:

The proposed definitions stated that the most current version of the ICD or DSM, respectively, would be the version applicable no earlier than the date that is 1 year before the first day of the applicable plan year; however, the proposed rules would permit the use of an updated version before the plan or issuer is required to use it. (p.25)

The reason this relatively simple choice of definition is a huge deal may be non-obvious. Let me help:

The DSM-5-TR is a wholly owned product of the American Psychiatric Association, which sounds like a medical guild, and it is. It’s a 501 © 3 non-profit, but financially, it’s a publisher of one book—that Diagnostic and Statistical Manual. I requested their financials about a year ago to see what was under the hood. They make about $8m annually by selling continuing medical education content (the APA annual meeting, for example). However, they make around $25 million annually from sales of the DSM. The APA has an elected assembly…that has no power to decide what happens to the $25m sales that are the DSM. That book’s contents are determined by a vote of these (currently) 23 people. They are the “Board of Trustees.”That book and these trustees draw the lines around which care must be covered equivalently to comply with everything else the DOL will outline in this series of articles.

To be blunt, MH/SUD hasn’t been covered similarly. Payers, historically, have bad mental health coverage. There have been barriers—in the parlance of the law, these are NQTLs. That’s “non-quantitative treatment limitations.” A.k.a. using obstacles to care, like prior authorization and stepped care models, to deny care in a sneaky way that could fly under the radar of regulators.

One way a plan could try to sneak previously is to keep an older version of a coverage standard, say by using a state-level standard that was loosey-goosey. The new rules try to put some harder limits on that, starting with definitions:

Consistent with this clarification, if a new version of the DSM is published in the middle of a plan year, plans and issuers will have at least one full year before they are required to use the updated version with respect to a plan year. For example, if a new version of the DSM is published on August 1, 2025, for a calendar year plan, that version of the DSM would be the most current version with respect to the plan year beginning on January 1, 2027.

At the very least, they must update their network assessment within a defined time frame to reflect the currently accepted standards for mental health problems.

Dementia and Autism are included—and those are two expensive diagnoses to manage. The inclusion of these will, I suspect, be crucial and at the expense of excellent treatment for the rest of the mental health conditions.

Eating disorders are also included—again, from the footnotes!

if a plan or an issuer offering group or individual health insurance coverage provides coverage for eating disorder benefits, including residential treatment, such group health plan or health insurance issuer shall provide such benefits consistent with the requirements of MHPAEA. (footnote 54, p. 27).

How about gender dysphoria? In keeping with the rubric above, since it’s listed in DSM and is an F-code diagnosis in ICDs system, the answer is…

Because the most current versions of both the ICD and DSM include gender dysphoria as a mental health condition as of the time of the issuance of these final rules, benefits for this condition are currently subject to the protections of MHPAEA and its implementing regulations, consistent with the framework described earlier in this preamble (p29).

As the next articles in this series will evaluate, part of the importance of what is “in” as a mental illness is crucial, given the metrics used to measure compliance. They will check to see if MH/SUD is similarly paid for, accessable, etc. This is, in part, a terrible standard. You can make MH/SUD coverage to achieve parity. One could also imagine a world where you made general medical and surgical care more awful to bring both into parity. It’s not outside of our imagination that payers could do that, too. The incentives for payers here, however, are crucial to remember. It’s not about “saving money,” as I’ve already explained north of 700 times. It’s about optimizing profits and medical loss ratio in some populations. Some payers are motivated by lower spending, such as in the self-funded employer part of the market.

Others need to make the math work on their remarkable profit machine. I’m a physician and an observer of the systems we now have in place. Another strategy to make MH/SUD parity happen? Just make it cost more! If you spend as much on MH/SUD care as you do on neurosurgery, the total cost of care goes up, and the parity check works out ok.

One expensive-enough drug or procedure for autism, Alzheimer’s, or any condition really could swing the balance in some plans. Parity is the standard Congress chose. Even if we meet that metric? Be careful what you wish for.
